title: How a Black Hole Bends Light
description: From starlight nudged by the Sun to light looping around a black hole, here is how gravity turns light into the ring we see.
question: How does a black hole bend light?

facts.claim: Around a non-spinning black hole, light can orbit at the photon sphere, 1.5 times the Schwarzschild radius (3GM/c²).
facts.note: Applies to the non-spinning (Schwarzschild) case. The 1.5 factor is the photon sphere's physical radius, not the apparent shadow radius.

facts.claim: A black hole's shadow looks at least about twice as wide as its event horizon, because gravity lenses the light around it.
facts.note: Sources differ in precision: NASA says about twice, one popular source says about 2.5, and the non-spinning calculation gives √27/2 ≈ 2.6 (shadow radius √27 GM/c² ≈ 5.2 GM/c²). 'More than twice' is the safe on-screen wording; use 2.6 only if labelled as the non-spinning theoretical value.

facts.claim: Far from a mass, general relativity gives a light-bending angle of 4GM/(c²b), twice the value from Newtonian gravity.
facts.note: b is how closely the ray passes the mass. This is only the weak-field limit and does not hold near the photon sphere.

facts.claim: As a light ray's path approaches the critical distance at the photon sphere, its bending angle grows without limit, so it can wrap around the black hole.
facts.value: logarithmic divergence at the critical impact parameter
facts.note: Rays passing just inside the critical distance are captured; rays just outside can loop around and escape.

facts.claim: Einstein's theory predicted that the Sun would shift a star's apparent position by 1.75 arcseconds for light grazing the Sun's rim.
Expeditions to Sobral, Brazil, and Príncipe observed the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919, to test light bending.
facts.note: Results were announced in London on November 6, 1919.

facts.claim: The 1919 expeditions reported star shifts of 1.98 arcseconds at Sobral and 1.61 arcseconds at Príncipe.
facts.note: Reported uncertainties are ±0.12 (Sobral) and ±0.3 (Príncipe). The handling of the data is contested: Eddington's decision to discard Sobral astrograph data is debated, though a 1979 plate remeasurement is reported as supporting the original analysis. Avoid saying the eclipse alone 'proved' Einstein right.

facts.claim: Gravity bends light from the far side of a black hole's disk over and under the hole, so the disk seems to form arcs above and below the shadow.
facts.value: far-side disk light appears above and below the shadow
facts.note: The effect is strongest when the disk is seen nearly edge-on. These arcs are separate from the photon ring.

facts.claim: Inside the disk's image is a thin photon ring, formed by light that has circled the black hole one or more times before escaping.
facts.note: The ring is really a set of progressively fainter, thinner rings from light making more orbits. This is not the broad bright ring in the EHT images, which could not resolve these thin subrings as a separate feature in the sources reviewed.

facts.claim: The first image of a black hole, M87*, was released by the Event Horizon Telescope on April 10, 2019.
facts.note: The image used data taken in April 2017 at a wavelength of 1.3 mm.

facts.claim: M87*'s bright ring measures 42 microarcseconds across on the sky.
facts.note: Published value is 42 ± 3 μas. Some popular sources round it to about 40.

facts.claim: M87*'s mass is about 6.5 billion times the Sun's.
M87* is more than 50 million light-years from Earth.
facts.note: Sources disagree slightly: 55 million light-years in EHT-era coverage, 53 million in another. The EHT analysis uses 16.8 Mpc, or about 55 million light-years.

facts.claim: The first image of Sagittarius A*, the Milky Way's central black hole, was released on May 12, 2022.
facts.note: Based on radio data taken in 2017.

facts.claim: Sagittarius A*'s ring of lensed light measures about 51.8 microarcseconds across on the sky.
facts.note: Listed as 51.8 ± 2.3 μas. One outlet mislabels this as the event horizon's size; it is the size of the lensed ring.

facts.claim: The size of Sagittarius A*'s ring matches the general relativity prediction based only on the black hole's mass and distance.
facts.value: ring diameter consistent with general relativity
facts.note: Mass is about 4.3 million Suns and distance about 27,000 light-years (Wikipedia: 4.297 ± 0.012 million solar masses; 26,996 ± 33 light-years).
